examples: I lent that book to my friend.
This morning I made a bento for my younger sister.
I will teach him Japanese.
I read a book to my child.
Shall I give you a ride to the station?

fields.explain:
A casual pattern, usually used between equals or close friends. With superiors or in business, avoid ～てあげる; use ～てさしあげる or a neutral expression instead.
Offering help: ～てあげましょうか can be perceived as "doing someone a favor" if the other person does not need it.
The recipient is always marked with に; the thing/matter helped with is marked with を/に/で depending on the verb.
Not used when the recipient is the speaker; in that case you must use ～てくれる/～てもらう.
Rarely used in formal written language; replace it with an expression that does not take credit for oneself.

• Expresses the action of "doing something for / helping" someone; the doer actively gives a benefit to another person.
• Point of view: from the giver's side. If the speaker is the recipient, use ～てくれる.
• The nuance ranges from friendly to slightly condescending, depending on the relationship. With superiors/customers, use ～てさしあげる (when talking about your own help) or rephrase.
• Can be used for both concrete and emotional actions: 勇気づけてあげる, 相談に乗ってあげる.
• Can express "no need / not worth doing for someone": ～てあげる必要はない／～てあげなくてもいい.
fields.notes:
• Tense/politeness follow the auxiliary verb あげる: あげる・あげます・あげた・あげようか.
• Do not combine it with honorific keigo (sonkeigo) toward the target at the same time (avoid 二重敬語).
• In advertising/services, "we do this for you" is usually avoided by emphasizing the customer's benefit without showing the agent.
meaning_vi: Do something for someone
explain: ◎ An expression showing that the speaker does something for someone.※Not used for people older than you
examples: 1. 赤ちゃんが寒そうだったので、毛布をかけてあげた。

2. 昨日、ワンさんの引っ越しを手伝ってあげた。

explain: Someone does something for someone else.
Not used when another person does something for you.
examples: 1. カリナさんは　おばあさんに　荷物を　運んであげます。

2. 日曜日、私は　母に　料理を　手伝ってあげます。

meaning_vi: The subject of the sentence is the speaker or someone psychologically close to the speaker. The recipient of the thing or action is not the speaker. When giving to a superior outside the family (such as a teacher, company president, customer, etc.), the pattern さしあげます is used.
examples: 1. ①妹はサラさんに花をあげました。
My younger sister gave Sarah flowers.
2. ②先生にカップを差し上げました。
I gave the teacher a cup.
3. ③サッカー場にいくの？地図を書いてあげるよ。
Are you going to the soccer field? I'll draw you a map.
～Vてもらいます and ～Vてくれます are both used when someone else does something for you. However, they differ in their subject.
In addition: •　～Vてくれます is only used for yourself and people close to you. •　～Vてもらいます expresses a stronger sense of gratitude.
giving and receiving

Used when an action brings a benefit to yourself or the other person.
1. 田中さんはチンさんに、漢字の読み方を教えてあげました。

Giving and receiving actions.
1. ①　見せてくれる、見せてあげる、見せてもらう
(someone) shows me, I show (someone), I get shown
2. ②　先生が旅行の写真を見せてくださった。
（＝先生(せんせい)に旅行(りょこう)の写真(しゃしん)を見(み)せていただいた。）

3. ③　隣の人が教科書を忘れたので、見せてあげた。

（＝隣(となり)の人(ひと)が見(み)せてくれた。）

mistakes: Using ～てあげる with a superior: change it to ～てさしあげる or another expression.
Wrong point of view: when the speaker is the recipient, you must use ～てくれる/～てもらう, not ～てあげる.
Forgetting に for the recipient: 彼に手伝ってあげる (correct), 彼手伝ってあげる (incorrect).
Offering too directly: 手伝ってあげます ⇒ may sound self-important; more neutral: お手伝いしましょうか.

fields.explain:
To emphasize gratitude, add ありがとうございました after the past-tense sentence.
With superiors/customers: prefer いただく to be humble.
に and から: both are possible; に is neutral/standard, から is casual/emphasizes the starting point.
Change it to the potential form (V-て もらえる) to turn it into "could you do this for me?" → a polite request.
The one receiving the benefit is usually 私/私たち (can be omitted). If it is someone else, state it clearly, and the context must show the speaker's point of view.

• Expresses "having someone do V for me/us," showing a benefit to the speaker or the speaker's group.
• The frame "N に V-て もらう" focuses on the recipient of the benefit (the speaker), unlike "N が V-て くれる," which focuses on the giver.
• Often carries a sense of gratitude, a request, or acknowledgment of help. With いただく, the nuance is humble and formal.
• The agent can be a person or an organization: 市役所に手続きをしてもらう（have city hall do the paperwork for you）.
• Not used for unintentional actions or actions with no clear doer. There must be an "agent" with volition/responsibility to do V.
fields.notes:
• In formal written language, you may see 〜ていただく with phrases like ご教示, ご確認, ご対応.
• Indirect "request": AさんにBさんを紹介してもらう（have A introduce B）; に is still used for the person doing the action.
• With organizations: 市に許可を出してもらう is natural because it is an "entity with authority." もらう is not used with inanimate things that have no will.
• When chaining several actions done for you: 連絡してもらって、資料も送ってもらった（they contacted me and also sent me the documents）.
meaning_vi: smiley1getsmiley2V done for you
explain: Someone received a helping action from someone else.
Vてもらいます is not used to say that another person received an action from you.
examples: 1. 私は　カリナさんに　スキーの　やり方を　教えてもらいました。
Karina taught me how to ski.
2. 私達は　店の人に　写真を　とってもらいました。
We had a shop employee take our picture.
meaning_vi: The subject (the one receiving the thing or the action) is the speaker or someone psychologically close to the speaker. When receiving from a superior outside the family, the pattern いただきます is used.
examples: 1. ①山田さんに／から時計をもらいました。
I received a watch from Mr. Yamada.
2. ②妹は先生に／から本をいただきました。
My younger sister received a book from her teacher.
3. ③サラさんに一緒に病院へ行ってもらった。
Sarah went to the hospital with me.
mistakes: Wrong point of view: "母が送ってもらった" is incorrect; it should be "母に送ってもらった".
Confusion with くれる: "田中さんが手伝ってくれた" is correct; with もらう it must be "田中さんに手伝ってもらった".
Using it with an inanimate agent: "雨にやませてもらった" is unnatural.
Forgetting the nuance of benefit: もらう always implies the speaker receives a benefit; it is not neutral like "AはBを直す".
On the JLPT, the trap is usually choosing between てくれる and てもらう based on the subject/point of view in the sentence.

examples: The sky is cloudy. It will probably rain soon.

He probably already knows, too.
Around when will they be back?
This movie is interesting, isn't it?
fields.explain:
A polite, neutral conjecture; suitable for business conversation and speeches.
Asking a polite question: ～でしょうか (softer than ～ますか).
Seeking agreement: ～でしょう？ (↑); sympathy: ～でしょうね (↓).
Goes well with adverbs: たぶん／おそらく／きっと＋～でしょう.
Not used with direct commands/prohibitions: ×「行きなさいでしょう」.

• Polite conjecture/estimate: about 70–80% certainty. Example: 彼は来るでしょう。
• Gently offers a personal judgment, avoiding a strong assertion. Natural in expert statements and weather forecasts.
• Asks for an opinion/conjecture politely with ～でしょうか.
• Seeks agreement/emphasizes something obvious with ～でしょう？ (rising intonation).
• Emphasizes sympathy/understanding with ～でしょうね／～でしょう（ね） (falling, soft intonation).
fields.notes:
• In formal written language, ～でしょう often appears in presentations and forecasts.
• Placed after a number to give an estimate: 30％でしょう (about 30%).
• Avoid using it many times in a short statement, as it can sound like you are avoiding responsibility.
• Expressive use: ～でしょう？ is casual; in formal settings use ～でしょうか／と思います.
meaning_vi: ～でしょう？:Right?
explain: Used to confirm something you were thinking, to double-check what you know, or to seek the other person's agreement.
The voice usually rises at the end of the sentence.
examples: 1. このりんご、おいしいでしょう？
This apple is delicious, isn't it?
2. あした　パーティーがあるでしょう？
There's a party tomorrow, right?
mistakes: Confusing it with a strong assertion: ～でしょう is still conjecture, not 100% certainty.
Using ～でしょう？ in formal settings can feel like forcing agreement.
Attaching it to commands/prohibitions is grammatically incorrect.
Confusing the degree: かもしれない (low) ＜ ～でしょう ＜ はずだ／に違いない (high).

fields.connection: Vます(drop ます) + 方 (書き方・使い方)
examples: Please teach me how to write kanji.
Do you know how to use this app?

I've gotten used to using chopsticks.
Let's review the way we do our work.

fields.explain:
Neutral; describes a general method: "how to do, how to use".
"仕方" is often used when talking about a "way/manner" with a nuance of evaluation (good/bad) or in set phrases:仕方がない.
Instructional texts and UIs often use ～方/～かた: ご利用のしかた,使い方ガイド.

• Turns a verb into a noun meaning "the way/style/method of doing V".
• When the direct object of V (with を) attaches to ～方, it usually becomes a noun phrase with の: 漢字を書く → 漢字の書き方.
• Particles for direction/destination/place such as へ/に/で stay as they are, because they belong to the structure of the original V: 駅への行き方, 鍋での作り方.
• ～方 is a noun and can combine with の, は, が, を, に like other nouns.
fields.notes:
• Spelling: しかた/仕方 are both correct; titles/instructions usually use 使い方/やり方.
• 来方 exists but is not very natural; people usually say 行き方 from the opposite direction.
• For verbs with two objects, consider simplifying: 日本語（の）勉強の仕方 as one large noun phrase.
meaning_vi: How to do…, the way to… (Vます+方)
mistakes: Wrong particle: ×漢字を書き方 → ○漢字の書き方.
Using 来方 when asking for directions: 行き方 is more natural.
Confusing ～方 with ～ように (purpose) in JLPT multiple-choice questions.
Wrong form: ×使う方 → ○使い方 (continuative form).

fields.meaning: Expresses Particle knowledge check | starting point
fields.explain:
N（時／年齢）＋から（starting point in time/age） means Indicates the starting point in time or age from which something begins or is valid.

Structure: N（時／年齢）＋から

This grammar pattern uses a noun indicating a specific time or age followed by から to express the point at which an action or state starts. For example, 18歳から means 'from 18 years old,' indicating that something becomes possible or valid starting at that age. It is commonly used to specify when a rule, permission, or event begins.

いいえ、ちがいます (fixed negative reply to deny correctness) means This phrase is used to politely and clearly deny or correct a statement, meaning 'No, that's not correct' or 'No, it is different.'

Structure: いいえ、ちがいます

The phrase combines いいえ (no) with ちがいます, the polite form of the verb ちがう (to differ, to be wrong), to deny a statement or correct a misunderstanding. It is a fixed negative reply commonly used when someone asks a question and the answer is negative. This expression is polite but not overly formal, suitable for everyday conversations and polite interactions.

fields.name: から（used at the end of a sentence）
examples: Someday I'll get back at you, you'll see.
Wait quietly, okay? I'll buy you a souvenir and bring it back.

A: I forgot to buy eggs.
B: It's fine, it's fine. More importantly, hurry up and wash your hands.
fields.explain: Used at the end of a sentence to express feelings such as a warning or comfort. A usage that expresses various kinds of appeals to the listener as an implication, without putting them into words. It is a form in which the underlined part of sentences such as 「いつかしかえししてやるから、覚えてろ」 and 「いいから、早く手を洗いなさい」 has been omitted or inverted. Used in spoken language.

fields.name: ちがいます（negative reply）
fields.meaning: ちがいます（否定返答） means The phrase ちがいます is used to indicate that something is incorrect or different, often as a polite negat
fields.explain:
ちがいます（否定返答） means The phrase ちがいます is used to indicate that something is incorrect or different, often as a polite negative response meaning 'No, that's not right' or 'No, that's different.'

Structure: Verb ちがう (to differ) in its polite present form ちがいます, used as a negative response to correct or deny a statement.

In conversation, when someone asks a question or makes a statement that is incorrect, responding with ちがいます politely denies or corrects the information. It is a common way to say 'No, that's not correct' without being rude.

examples: From now on, it is you who will protect this shop and help it grow.

fields.name: のです（explanation）
fields.connection: plain form + のです / N・Na + なのです
examples: I'm sorry I'm late. You see, I got caught in a traffic jam on the way.

fields.name: まだ（continuing from the past）
examples: It's already been a week, but my father and mother are still fighting.
There was a big earthquake when I was a child. Even now, I still remember that time clearly.
Even into this year, the Japanese economy continues to stagnate.
Unlike in the past, people in their 60s are still young.
It's September, but it's still hot.
Sanae may talk like a big shot, but she's still a child, isn't she?
fields.explain: Often used in the form 「まだＶ－ている」 to express that the same state has continued all along. 5. uses the form 「まだＶ一ていた」 and expresses that, although things are different now, the state was continuing at some point in the past. It means 「今 はいないけれど、そのころは生きていた」. ⑦～⑨ emphasize that the present remains in the same state as before and has not reached the next stage it should naturally reach. （７） means 「もう夏も終わつて涼しくなっていい頃なのに、そうなっていない」, ⑧ means 「大人に至っていない」, and ⑨ means 「お酒がゆるされる年齢に達していない」.

fields.name: まだ（continuing until completion）
examples: From now on, it will get even colder.
The rain will probably continue for another two or three days.
It seems the economy will not improve for some time yet.
This stock will rise in price even more.
The hard part is still ahead of us.
fields.explain: Expresses that the current state will continue from now on. Using 「まだまだ」 gives the meaning 「さらにもっと」「もっともっと」, expressing that the degree will become higher or that something will continue for a long time. When there is a word expressing a definite period such as 「二、三日」「三日」, as in 2., 「まだまだ」 cannot be used.

fields.name: まだ（comparison）
examples: Rather than being made to write a long report that takes days, an exam that's over in one day is still better.
I hate all housework, but laundry is still better than cleaning.
I lost my house and everything I owned in this earthquake, but at least I survived, so I'm still lucky.

A: Ugh, I hate this. I have five exams.
B: You're still better off. I have 11.
fields.explain: Used in forms such as 「まだいい」「まだましだ」 to mean that neither is good, but one is a little better than the other.（５４２）
